::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) may provide a communication option for people with severe motor impairment, when conventional assistive access becomes unreliable.

To date, several potential improvements of BCI-related hardware and software components have been investigated, for instance, classification algorithms for brain signals such as electroencephalography (EEG).
These efforts focused on laboratory work with healthy participants.
However, this is not representative for real-life conditions of potential motorimpaired end-users with diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

Our study compares state-of-the-art classification approaches on a real-life dataset of an end-user with ALS in the locked-in state (LIS) and a tactile P300-based BCI, obtained during long-term home-use.
We applied classifiers, including Shrinkage Linear Discriminant Analysis (ShrinkLDA) and Riemannian Geometry Classifiers (RGC).
We tested effects of different calibration scenarios (i.e., amount of training data, time between calibration) and spatial filtering (xDawn).
These variations were compared to the results of a Stepwise Linear Discriminant Analysis (SWLDA), the classifier used during the original online recordings and reimplemented here as the reference.
We defined an accuracy of >70% as sufficient performance (based on prior work).
text.formatted: We defined an accuracy of >70% as sufficient performance (based on prior work).

text.text: SWLDA could be outperformed, but without spatial filtering with xDawn, no classification algorithm allowed for sufficient independent home-use, with accuracies ranging between 33% to 66%; SWLDA: 59%.
The addition of spatial filtering via xDawn notably improved classification results for most classifiers, with the best performance (73%) achieved by classifiers using Riemannian Geometry.
For some tangent space support vector machine (SVM) approaches, xDawn decreased performance.
No tested classifier achieved consistent accuracy of >70% known as a minimum threshold for meaningful communication via assistive technology.
text.formatted: No tested classifier achieved consistent accuracy of >70% known as a minimum threshold for meaningful communication via assistive technology.

text.text: This is the first study comparing classifiers on a large set of tactile P300-based BCI data obtained from an end-user in the LIS in his own home.
Of the state-of-the-art classifiers, only four tested classifiers were able to reach slightly beyond an average accuracy of >70%.
text.formatted: Of the state-of-the-art classifiers, only four tested classifiers were able to reach slightly beyond an average accuracy of >70%.

text.text: No classifier performed consistently above this threshold.

Future work can build on our findings by investigating how disease characteristics, hardware and software optimization, and environmental factors influence BCI signal classification under real-life conditions for potential end-users with severe motor impairment including the LIS.
The locked-in state (LIS) can be defined as the state of a conscious mind in a paralyzed body.

Although terminology varies across publications, we adopt "state" as a broader designation encompassing different underlying conditions, while using "syndrome" for the traditional clinical presentation associated with brainstem injury.
The term "locked-in syndrome" was introduced by Plum and Posner in 1966 (Posner et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The term "locked-in syndrome" was introduced by <ref type="bibr">Plum and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Posner in 1966 (Posner et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas in classic LIS only vertical movement of the eyes and eyelids remain, in complete or total LIS (CLIS) no voluntary muscle movement is possible (Bauer et al., 1979).
text.formatted: Whereas in classic LIS only vertical movement of the eyes and eyelids remain, in complete or total LIS (CLIS) no voluntary muscle movement is possible <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bauer et al., 1979)</ref>.

text.text: (C)LIS is not caused by a singular disease, but may have several causes, most commonly vascular complications, traumatic brain injuries or demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis, and neurodegenerative motor neuron disease such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Patterson and Grabois, 1986; Lulé et al., 2009; Schnetzer et al., 2023).

text.text: In the LIS, patients retain the potential ability to use an eye-tracker for communication, but this ability is challenged during the transition to complete LIS.
The potential independence from muscular activity renders braincomputer interfaces (BCIs) one of the last communication options in CLIS (Kübler et al., 2001a).

text.text: In the past, various BCIs for communication have been proposed, active (e.g., based on motorimagery, slow cortical potentials (Kübler et al., 1999; Neuper et al., 2006; Saeedi et al., 2017)) as well as reactive (i.e., based on event-related potentials (ERPs) (Farwell and Donchin, 1988; Nijboer et al., 2008) or visual evoked potentials (VEPs) (Wang et al., 2008; Bin et al., 2009 Bin et al., , 2011;; Spüler et al., 2012)).

text.text: The P300-based BCI remains one of the most frequently used candidates (Allison et al., 2020).

text.text: It utilizes a positive ERP response associated with attending to a task-relevant salient target stimulus in an oddball paradigm, where it is usually presented in a randomized order and less frequently with additional task-irrelevant and more frequently presented non-target stimuli (Wascher et al., 2020).

text.text: The highest information transfer rates (ITR) are typically achieved in visual paradigms (Kaufmann and Kübler, 2014; Allison et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2022).

text.text: However, the progressive loss of control over ocular muscles and eyelids is considered detrimental for visual paradigms (Brunner et al., 2010), making them less feasible for potential end-users (Pires et al., 2022).

text.text: Hence, gazeindependent paradigms such as auditory or tactile P300-based BCIs have been investigated (Kübler et al., 2009; Riccio et al., 2012; Herweg et al., 2016; Eidel and Kübler, 2020; Ziebell et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2021; Séguin et al., 2024).

text.text: While patients are the main target group for the proposed devices, they have rarely been included in studies (Kübler, 2020; Peters et al., 2022; Rezvani et al., 2024).

text.text: To target this issue, a growing body of work on user-centered design has been conducted to consider the needs and opinions of potential end-users at every step of BCI development (Vaughan et al., 2006; Sellers et al., 2010; Schreuder et al., 2013; Kübler et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2017; Bettencourt et al., 2024).

text.text: For instance, long-term independent home-use studies have evaluated and optimized several BCI applications, including the visual P300-based Brain Painting software (Botrel et al., 2015; Holz et al., 2015a Holz et al., , 2015b)), audiovisual P300-based communication paradigms for a patient in a CLIS and a tactile P300-based BCI (Ziebell et al., 2024).

text.text: Predominantly, these studies have focused on collecting and implementing objective and subjective measures on the usability criteria effectiveness (e.g., online accuracy), efficiency (e.g., ITR), and satisfaction (e.g., rating scales).
Complementary to this focus on the comprehensive assessment of usability measures, it has been suggested to optimize BCIs based on signal characteristics (Han et al., 2022).

text.text: Signal-based optimizations could for example include improving the signal quality through training (Eidel and Kübler, 2022), identifying user states beneficial for BCI performance using electrophysiological features, for instance via Lempel-Ziv complexity (Settgast and Kübler, 2024), or testing alternative signal classification algorithms (Huang et al., 2021).

text.text: In particular with regard to signal classification algorithms, a plethora of BCI-related studies were published in recent years -however, this work has so far been mostly directed at optimizing signal classifiers for data of healthy participants in laboratory conditions (Lotte et al., 2007 (Lotte et al., , 2018;; Peters et al., 2022; Rezvani et al., 2024).

text.text: Notably, classifiers such as Linear Discriminant Analysis with a shrinkage parameter (ShrinkLDA) and Riemannian Geometry Classifiers (RGCs) have demonstrated promising performance (Blankertz et al., 2011; Lotte, 2015; Congedo et al., 2017; Yger et al., 2017; Lotte et al., 2018), reaching higher accuracies than more traditional approaches such as Stepwise Linear Discriminant Analysis (SWLDA) while minimizing computational demands.

text.text: Further strength lies in their capability to deal with little training data.
As an additional example, spatial filtering, for instance via xDawn has been identified as a tool with substantial potential (Rivet et al., 2009 (Rivet et al., , 2011)).

text.text: As a next step in line with the hitherto reviewed literature, a major current challenge remains in testing the reliability of such promising classifier methods on end-user data, since diseases as well as circumstances of home use may influence data distribution in terms of lower signal to noise ratio and higher variance (Bettencourt et al., 2024).

text.text: The aim of this study was to test a selection of state-of-the-art signal classification algorithms on a previously collected large dataset that was long-term recorded from an end-user in the LIS at his own home.
In related work, where additional details can be found, this dataset has been analyzed with a focus on the long-term persistence of the P300 (Ziebell et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In related work, where additional details can be found, this dataset has been analyzed with a focus on the long-term persistence of the P300 <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Ziebell et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: More specifically, we were interested in whether promising algorithms such as ShrinkLDA, MDM, FGMDM, tangent-space logistic regression and SVMs, and combinations with spatial filtering via xDawn may improve the performance baseline established with SWLDA.
The end-user of the BCI (WT) is a male electrical engineer, who was 58 years at the time when the relevant data collection for this paper began.
He was diagnosed with ALS ten years prior (October 2010) and has been in the LIS since 2015 (Revised Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Functional Rating Scale; ALSFRS-R=0, (Cedarbaum et al., 1999)).
text.formatted: He was diagnosed with ALS ten years prior (October 2010) and has been in the LIS since 2015 (Revised Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Functional Rating Scale; ALSFRS-R=0, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cedarbaum et al., 1999)</ref>).

text.text: He receives invasive mechanical ventilation by tracheostomy and nourishment via a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy.
WT was able to communicate via eyeblinks, eye-movements, and pressure detection on his leg throughout the entire study.

Usually, he relies on eye tracking in combination with assistive software, such as Dasher (http://www.inference.org.uk/dasher/) and GRID 3 (https://thinksmartbox.com/product/grid-3/), to operate his computer, which was his preferred communication device.
text.formatted: Usually, he relies on eye tracking in combination with assistive software, such as Dasher (<ref type="url" target="http://www.inference.org.uk/dasher/">http://www.inference.org.uk/dasher/</ref>) and GRID 3 (<ref type="url" target="https://thinksmartbox.com/product/grid-3/">https://thinksmartbox.com/product/grid-3/</ref>), to operate his computer, which was his preferred communication device.

text.text: WT reported this way of communication as increasingly exhausting, as eye movement became difficult.

In February 2021, i.e., four months after the start of the relevant data collection for this paper, the patient was further diagnosed with sensory neuropathy in his legs, which led to an adaptation of the experimental setup.
WT has been interested in BCI testing since 2016 and had his first tests with a tactile P300-based BCI in 2018 (Ziebell et al., 2024).
text.formatted: WT has been interested in BCI testing since 2016 and had his first tests with a tactile P300-based BCI in 2018 <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Ziebell et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The protocol was conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Ethics Committee of the Psychological Institute of the University of Würzburg (approval number: GZEK 2013-1/GZEK 2021-53).
The data collection was guided by the user-centered design approach (Kübler et al., 2014) and is one of the rare instances of a long-term use of a BCI in a patient's own home.
text.formatted: The data collection was guided by the user-centered design approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Kübler et al., 2014)</ref> and is one of the rare instances of a long-term use of a BCI in a patient's own home.

text.text: It was part of a cooperation between the Nuremberg Institute of Technology Georg Simon Ohm and the University of Würzburg, for developing devices to assist people with severe motor impairment.
This particular project aimed at improving the tactile P300-based BCI paradigm to achieve gaze-independent control of communication software presented on a computer.
In the current study, we focused on data that was collected in 39 sessions, starting November 13 th , 2020 and ending May 31 st 2021.
The first two months included three sessions per week, the remaining months included typically one session per week.
Initially, the hardware was set up by staff of the University of Würzburg at the home of the patient.
Until session 13 (December 14 th , 2020), the caregivers were introduced to the experimental setup so that they could prepare the setup independently.
This was a considerable advantage during the COVID-19 pandemic.
In addition, the sessions were supervised and controlled remotely by the authors via the remote service software AnyDesk (https://www.anydesk.com/).
text.formatted: In addition, the sessions were supervised and controlled remotely by the authors via the remote service software AnyDesk (<ref type="url" target="https://www.anydesk.com/">https://www.anydesk.com</ref>).

text.text: The paradigm used here has been established in prior work (Kaufmann et al., 2014; Herweg et al., 2016; Eidel and Kübler, 2020, 2022; Ziebell et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The paradigm used here has been established in prior work <ref type="bibr">(Kaufmann et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Herweg et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Eidel and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kübler, 2020, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Ziebell et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In our analysis, we focused on a tactile P300-based BCI paradigm with six classes.

In this paradigm, six vibrotactile stimulators (T1, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6) were placed on shoulders (T1/2), elbows or wrist joints (T3/4) and ankles, knee pits or thighs (T5/6) (see Figure1A) to elicit P300 responses.
After the patient was diagnosed with sensory neuropathy in the legs, the placement was adapted and the lower limb positions were moved on the torso, T5 on the chest and T6 on the neck (see Figure1B).
To assess BCI performance we used a copy-spelling task as pioneered by prior work and described there in more detail (Kübler et al., 2001b).
text.formatted: To assess BCI performance we used a copy-spelling task as pioneered by prior work and described there in more detail <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kübler et al., 2001b)</ref>.

text.text: In brief, during each response selection trial, the patient was visually instructed to focus on one specific target tactor, which he should select accurately (or in terms of the copy-spelling task, copy accurately) by using the BCI.
During a stimulation sequence, tactors vibrated for 220 ms in a randomly counterbalanced order, with an interstimulus interval of 400 ms.
One trial consisted of ten (calibration) or eight (copy) activations of each of the six tactors.
One run comprised six trials, each tactor being the target once, resulting in 60 target and 300 nontarget epochs per calibration run.
Each training session started with three calibration runs and was followed by three copy runs.
After that, the patient could freely choose to continue testing the BCI for an undetermined number of more runs.
To allow for a standardized comparability, those additional freely chosen runs were excluded from analysis.
In the copy runs, the patient was instructed to focus on a specific tactor and received feedback on the classification result.
This classification was based on a SWLDA, which was calibrated based on the data from the calibration runs.
The BCI cycle was controlled by BCI2000 (Schalk et al., 2004), connected wirelessly to an Arduino (Adafruit HUZZAH32 ESP32 Feather) which controlled the tactors.
text.formatted: The BCI cycle was controlled by BCI2000 <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Schalk et al., 2004)</ref>, connected wirelessly to an Arduino (Adafruit HUZZAH32 ESP32 Feather) which controlled the tactors.

text.text: The soft-and hardware for the Arduino was specifically developed for this use case.
EEG signal was recorded with twelve Ag/AgCl g.Ladybird active electrodes (g.tec Engineering GmbH, Graz, Austria).

The electrodes were positioned according to the 10-10 system, first in positions of SetA (Fz, FC1, FC2, C3, Cz, C4, P3, Pz, P4, O1, Oz, and O2) and were later moved to focus around Cz (SetB: Fz, FC1, FC2, C1, C3, Cz, C2, C4, CP1, CPz, CP2, Pz; after session 11 on December12 th 2020) as signal strength of the P300 was higher in locations closer to Cz.
Reference and ground were placed on the right earlobe and AFz.
All data was recorded using BCI2000 (Schalk et al., 2004) with a sampling rate of 512 Hz, a bandpass-filter from 0.1 to 60 Hz, and a notch-filter from 48 to 52 Hz.
text.formatted: All data was recorded using BCI2000 <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Schalk et al., 2004)</ref> with a sampling rate of 512 Hz, a bandpass-filter from 0.1 to 60 Hz, and a notch-filter from 48 to 52 Hz.

text.text: As in previous studies (Herweg et al., 2016; Eidel and Kübler, 2020; Eidel et al., 2021; Ziebell et al., 2024), the focus in the physiological analysis was on the electrode positions Fz, Cz and Pz.
text.formatted: As in previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Herweg et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Eidel and Kübler, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Eidel et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Ziebell et al., 2024)</ref>, the focus in the physiological analysis was on the electrode positions Fz, Cz and Pz.

text.text: The data was filtered with a band pass (0.1 -40 Hz) and baseline corrected (subtracting the mean of the 100 ms pre-stimulus).
Epochs, which contained a peak-to-peak amplitude of 100 µV or higher were excluded.
Visual inspection of the data suggested an increased latency, hence, the critical time window for evaluating the P300 was shifted to 350 -600 ms.

Although a positive deflection was maintained longer than 600 ms the window was chosen in this manner because best discriminability (predicted by R²) was expected in said window and further elongation would have also increased the overlap with subsequent stimuli.

A SWLDA, provided by BCI2000 (Schalk et al., 2004) represented the current classifier of the device, therefore, a Python SWLDA implementation was considered as a reference for all other tested algorithms.

text.text: All classifiers were implemented in Python 3.7.13, using the machine-learning library scikit learn 1.0.2, the framework for MEG and EEG analysis MNE 0.23.0 and the toolbox for signal classification with Riemannian Geometry pyRiemann 0.2.7.
For the implementation of the SWLDA, code from a git repository of Stocks was adapted (https://github.com/taliastocks/Py3GUI).
text.formatted: For the implementation of the SWLDA, code from a git repository of Stocks was adapted (<ref type="url" target="https://github.com/taliastocks/Py3GUI">https://github.com/taliastocks/Py3GUI</ref>).

text.text: The regular LDA and the ShrinkLDA were applied using the predefined function of the scikit-learn framework.
The regularization parameter was determined by the Ledoit-Wolf optimization algorithm (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004).
text.formatted: The regularization parameter was determined by the Ledoit-Wolf optimization algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Ledoit and Wolf, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: For the RGCs, the covariance matrices and respective classification results were calculated using the functions provided by the pyRiemann-toolbox.

Five covariance-based classification approaches were implemented: minimum distance to mean (MDM), MDM preceded by Fisher geodesic discriminant analysis (FGMDM), tangent-space classification using logistic regression (TS_LG), a linear-kernel support-vector machine (TS_SVM_lin), or a radial-basisfunction-kernel support-vector machine (TS_SVM_rbf).
The FGDA is an adaptation of Fisher's Linear Discriminant Analysis to tangent space (Barachant et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The FGDA is an adaptation of Fisher's Linear Discriminant Analysis to tangent space <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Barachant et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: RGCs rely on spatial covariance matrices for classification.
Logistic regression (TS_LG) used an L1 penalty and the liblinear solver.
To assure the covariance matrices were symmetric positive-definite, they were regularized, again with the parameter determined by the criterion of Ledoit and Wolf (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004).
text.formatted: To assure the covariance matrices were symmetric positive-definite, they were regularized, again with the parameter determined by the criterion of <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Ledoit and Wolf (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Due to the use of spatial covariance matrices, the computational complexity of the RGCs was not influenced by temporal resolution.
MDM, FGMDM and the three tangent-space classifiers were evaluated using covariance representations derived from both the original sampling rate and data resampled to 20 Hz.
Approaches using resampled data are marked with the suffix "_res", and approaches using spatial filtering are marked with "_xDawn"
To increase the signal-to-noise ratio we introduced spatial filtering with the xDawn algorithm (Rivet et al., 2009).
text.formatted: To increase the signal-to-noise ratio we introduced spatial filtering with the xDawn algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Rivet et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, it increases the computational demands, calibration time and induces the dual optimization problem, i.e., the independent tuning of the filter and classifier.

To address the issue of increased computational demands and calibration time the filter decomposed the signal into two components per class, yielding a reduction of 2/3 of the former signal in both classification approaches.

LDA, ShrinkLDA and SWLDA were each evaluated with and without xDawn; MDM, FGMDM, TS_LG, TS_SVM_lin and TS_SVM_rbf were each evaluated with and without xDawn and temporal resampling, yielding 26 classifiers.
To sustain comparability with BCI2000, epochs were down sampled to 20 Hz in all implementations, except mentioned otherwise.
Accordingly, the time window of the epoch remained 0 -800 ms after stimulus onset.
All python scripts used for the data classifications are available online (https://github.com/iamraP/P300ClassifierComparison.git).

text.text: Classifiers were trained using the calibration runs specified for each of the four conditions below.
The accuracy of each training session was evaluated independently on the three copy runs.
To further increase the relevance for the use case, it was attempted to approximate an online classification process.
Therefore, target-class probabilities were estimated for each tactor and for individual epoch and averaged across its eight stimulus repetitions within each selection.
The tactor with the highest cumulative probability was selected as the overall classification result of the respective trial.
For the calibration itself, four conditions were tested:

Sessionwise Calibration -3 Runs (Sess3): For each session, the classifiers were retrained using the three calibration runs of the same day (180 target trials) to account for possible changes in between sessions, which corresponded to the paradigm applied during data acquisition.

Sessionwise Calibration -1 Run (Sess1): For each session, the classifiers were retrained only using the first calibration run of that day (60 target trials) to still account for possible changes between sessions, but also to test classification performance with limited training data.

To assess classifier transferability and performance stability across sessions, we applied the existing classifier from the first available session (180 target trials) to all sessions with the same setup.

This was done separately for the two electrode configurations: For electrode SetA, classifiers were trained on the calibration data of the first day and evaluated on copy runs from that day and subsequent sessions using SetA.
The same was done for SetB.
Here, the classifiers were calibrated on the data of the first session after the switch.
To account for some expected variance in the data between sessions, the classifiers were trained on the first three sessions (540 target trials) with the corresponding electrode setup.

For an individual session comprising 18 six-choice selections, at least seven correct selections (38.9% accuracy) exceeded chance in an unadjusted one-sided exact binomial test at α = 0.05, assuming independent selections with chance probability 1/6 (Billinger et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For an individual session comprising 18 six-choice selections, at least seven correct selections (38.9% accuracy) exceeded chance in an unadjusted one-sided exact binomial test at α = 0.05, assuming independent selections with chance probability 1/6 <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Billinger et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Three Sess1 SWLDA fits failed to produce a classifier.
These sessions were assigned with zero accuracy in the summaries and inferential analyses, retaining all 39 sessions for each approach.
All statistical analyses were conducted with the programming language R. Classifiers were compared against each other within each calibration condition.

To accommodate non-normally distributed accuracies and the evaluation of all classifier approaches on the same 39 sessions, we used nonparametric Friedman tests with session as the blocking factor, followed by two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
If alpha correction was necessary, we applied the Bonferroni method.

As a criterion for successful performance, we defined an accuracy beyond 70%, since accuracies beyond 70% have traditionally been described as sufficient to operate relevant communication software (Kübler et al., 2001b).

text.text: With three calibration runs per session (Sess3), SWLDA achieved a mean accuracy of 59% (SD: 20%).
Four configurations significantly outperformed this reference, all incorporating xDawn.
Tangent-space logistic regression with xDawn achieved the highest mean accuracy (73%, SD: 16%), followed by FGMDM with xDawn (72%, SD: 17%).

FGMDM and tangent-space logistic regression with xDawn each achieved 62% accuracy (SD: 20% and 19%, respectively), exceeding SWLDA by approximately 18 pp (both p < .001).

With calibration based on three runs from one session (Trans1), mean accuracy was lower than in Sess3 for all 26 configurations, with an average decrease of 10 pp across configurations.

FGMDM with xDawn had the highest mean accuracy (66%, SD: 19%), exceeding SWLDA by 16 pp (p = .002; r = .72).

The average increase across configurations was 9 pp; the exceptions were resampled minimum-distance-to-mean classification and linear-kernel tangent-space support-vector classification with xDawn.

text.text: Matched comparisons isolated the effect of adding xDawn to each classifier configuration.
Across the four calibration conditions, xDawn increased mean accuracy in 9-12 of the 13 matched pairs, although the statistical evidence for these improvements varied by classifier and condition.
Both the original and resampled minimum-distance-to-mean classifiers improved significantly with xDawn in every calibration condition (all p ≤ .030).
FGMDM and tangent-space logistic regression without temporal resampling showed significant improvements under Sess3, Sess1, and Trans1, but PREPRINT not under Trans3.
For SWLDA mean accuracy increased with xDawn in all four conditions, but none of the matched comparisons was significant after correction (Supplementary Tables 2 3 4 5).

text.text: Spatial filtering reduced accuracy for some tangent-space support-vector configurations.
In Trans3, the linear-kernel variant decreased from 66% without xDawn to 40% with xDawn (p < .001), and its resampled counterpart decreased from 56% to 39% (p = .001).

Three configurations in Sess3 and four in Trans3 achieved mean accuracies above the study's 70% criterion; all of these configurations used xDawn.
However, no configuration exceeded 70% in every evaluated session under any calibration condition (Figures 4 5 6 7).

Under Sess1, 10 of the 26 configurations achieved or tied for the highest accuracy in at least one session and the lowest accuracy in at least one other session (Figure 8).

text.text: Improvements in mean accuracy therefore coexisted with substantial variation in performance across recording days.
Here we provide the first comparison of state-of-the-art signal classification algorithms on long-term home-use data from an ALS end-user in the LIS who used a tactile P300-based BCI (author WT).

In related work, we provided first analyses of these data with a focus on the ability of WT to persistently produce a P300-like ERP pattern based on ideas from the user-centered design (Ziebell et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In related work, we provided first analyses of these data with a focus on the ability of WT to persistently produce a P300-like ERP pattern based on ideas from the user-centered design <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Ziebell et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the spirit of expanding this earlier user-centered work by focusing on optimizing signal classification (Han et al., 2022) and based on the stability of WT's P300 ERP component, we evaluated selected algorithms such as ShrinkLDA, RGCs, tangent-space logistic regression and SVMs, as well as a traditional SWLDA (which also has been used in prior work with WT) in combination with spatial filtering via xDawn.

text.text: As seen in previous studies target and non-target were best separable at central electrodes, where a typical P300 pattern was observed (predicted by R² ) (Ziebell et al., 2024).

text.text: Notably, even though in WT a P300 could be persistently elicited, we found a high variance of amplitude and online accuracy, which is why it was of special interest to us whether alternative signal classification algorithms could have optimized WT's BCI performance in hindsight and for potential future work.
As a measure of performance, we aimed for accuracies >70% which have traditionally been described as a minimum for meaningful communication via assistive technology (Kübler et al., 2001b).
text.formatted: As a measure of performance, we aimed for accuracies >70% which have traditionally been described as a minimum for meaningful communication via assistive technology <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kübler et al., 2001b)</ref>.

text.text: We could show that some of the newer classifiers could improve the results achieved by the SWLDA.
The strongest candidates were FGMDM_xDawn and the xDawn-based tangent-space logistic-regression approaches; FGMDM_res_xDawn was also competitive, particularly in Trans3.

Online information transfer rates (ITRs) ranged from 0.11 bits/min to 3.69 bits/min, the maximum session accuracy was 100%, corresponding to a theoretical ITR of 5.21 bits/min under the existing six-choice, eight-repetition paradigm.

Whereas the ShrinkLDA_xDawn has minimal computational costs, in comparison, the FGMDM_xDawn and FGMDM_res_xDawn are among the more computational demanding of the tested classifiers because they use two kinds of filters.
Nonetheless, both should be feasible online, as the calibration and classification of an entire training day remained well under a minute on a conventional laptop.

As expected from earlier work (Lotte and Guan, 2009; Delgado et al., 2020), the classification accuracy decreased for almost all classifiers when fewer calibration data were included (we tested three runs with 180 target trials versus one run with 60 target trials).
text.formatted: As expected from earlier work <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Lotte and Guan, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Delgado et al., 2020)</ref>, the classification accuracy decreased for almost all classifiers when fewer calibration data were included (we tested three runs with 180 target trials versus one run with 60 target trials).

text.text: The exceptions were MDM_res whose mean accuracy remained approximately stable and whereas TS_SVM_lin_xDawn and TS_SVM_lin_res_xDawn even improved.
For instance, SWLDA accuracy decreased by 25% (relative).
Likely the distribution of the data, sampled in a single run, is not representative for the specific day it was collected on, as attention, noise or electrode contact quality may vary.
Most classification results improved further with spatial filtering via xDawn, which increases the signal-tonoise ratio and hence facilitates the estimation of the true distribution of the data.

This is particularly relevant for real-life end-user settings, where occurrence of confounding noise is of higher likelihood than in laboratory settings that allow for stricter noise control (Bettencourt et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This is particularly relevant for real-life end-user settings, where occurrence of confounding noise is of higher likelihood than in laboratory settings that allow for stricter noise control <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bettencourt et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Among classifiers without xDawn, FGMDM showed the smallest decrease from Sess3 to Trans1 (3.3pp), whereas several classifiers improved from Sess3 to Trans3.
FGMDM_xDawn achieved the highest mean accuracy in both transfer conditions: 66% in Trans1 and 73% in Trans3.
In Trans3 the 70%-threshold was also exceeded by TS_LG_res_xDawn (72%), TS_LG_xDawn (72%) and FGMDM_res_xDawn (71%).
The lower Trans1 accuracies relative to Sess3 may reflect limited generalization of models and filters fitted to one calibration session.
Training on a limited set of sessions may restrict generalization to other sessions.

Averaged across the 13 matched classifier pairs, xDawn increased mean accuracy in each condition, although individual SVM approaches sometimes performed worse, with significant decreases for TS_SVM_lin_res in Sess3, Trans1 and Trans3, and for TS_SVM_lin in Trans3.
A possible account for poorer SVM performance is that fixed filtering and SVM settings were less suitable together or that useful information was lost.

Future work should investigate them by jointly varying the number of xDawn components and SVM hyperparameters within validation restricted to the training data, while keeping evaluation data held out.
FGMDM, which performed lower than SWLDA in both session-wise calibration approaches, was significantly enhanced by the preceding xDawn in three conditions.
FGMDM_xDawn achieved higher mean accuracy than both SWLDA and SWLDA_xDawn in all calibration conditions.
For SWLDA, xDawn increased mean accuracy in every calibration condition, but none of these matched comparisons was significant after the within-condition Bonferroni correction.
This may be due to the fact that the regularization of the covariance as well as the stepwise feature selection already counteracts the background noise of the acquired signal.

The Riemannian approaches without xDawn showed heterogeneous performance, with the lowest accuracies for MDM_res and considerably higher Trans3 accuracies for FGMDM and tangent-space logistic regression.

While in other studies these approaches could hold up or even outperform other state-of-the-art classifiers (Barachant and Congedo, 2014; Delgado et al., 2020), the MDM underperformed in this dataset.
text.formatted: While in other studies these approaches could hold up or even outperform other state-of-the-art classifiers <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barachant and Congedo, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Delgado et al., 2020)</ref>, the MDM underperformed in this dataset.

text.text: This might be explained by the partially malfunctioning electrode and further supports the combination of classifiers with spatial filters.
While MDM only maps the data to the manifold, it does not perform a feature selection and is therefore imperiled to distortion by such issues (i.e., bad channels).
Overall, we observed a high variance of the classification accuracy.
Although several classifier approaches achieved mean accuracies above 70%, no variant exceeded this threshold in every evaluated session under any of the four calibration conditions.

Thus, none consistently met the PREPRINT study's performance criterion across all recording days, indicating that the improvements in average accuracy did not establish reliable day-to-day performance.
Interestingly, performance rankings were inconsistent, and no single classifier always outperformed the others.
This means the variations in data distribution had different effects on the different approaches.
This indicates that there might not be the "one" classifier that always yields the best possible classification result.
More likely, depending on factors, which can vary from session to session and patient to patient, different classifiers will perform best.
The observed day-to-day variability may reflect several physiological, technical and environmental influences.
Potential contributors include changes in psychological factors such as attention, fatigue or mental workload (Han et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Potential contributors include changes in psychological factors such as attention, fatigue or mental workload <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Han et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These influences could affect classifier configurations differently because of their different signal representations, spatial filtering and regularization strategies.
For example, spatial filtering and covariance regularization can affect ERP classification performance (Blankertz et al., 2011; Rivet et al., 2011).

text.text: It is therefore plausible that session-dependent changes in target-non-target separability, channel-specific noise, and ERP timing contributed to the observed changes in classifier rankings.
However, the present analysis did not isolate these factors or their interactions.
In related work, we have provided first steps toward more detailed investigations in such directions (Ziebell et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In related work, we have provided first steps toward more detailed investigations in such directions <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Ziebell et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should assess signal quality, recording conditions and user state alongside classification accuracy in further detail to evaluate potential systematic influences of such factors on performance variability across recording days for individual end-users.
The feasibility of these classifiers for online use remains to be established.
On a regular laptop the computation time stayed well within limits (M: 7.42s, SD: 13.71s, for both, calibration and classification of data of an entire session).

End-to-end processing time for the updated implementations remains to be measured on the intended hardware, including data preparation, covariance estimation, spatial filtering, model fitting and prediction.
The present classifier comparison is conditional on the selected preprocessing pipeline.
Recent multiverse evidence indicates that filtering, referencing, baseline correction, and artifact handling can substantially alter EEG decoding performance (Kessler et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent multiverse evidence indicates that filtering, referencing, baseline correction, and artifact handling can substantially alter EEG decoding performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kessler et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Future work should test whether the observed classifier ranking remains stable across plausible preprocessing choices, particularly for noisy home recordings.
Further, no systematic hyperparameter tuning was performed for the classifiers.
The performance differences observed therefore apply to the evaluated configurations and may not reflect the best attainable performance of each approach.
Hyperparameter optimization could alter both absolute accuracies and the relative ranking of classifiers.
Although WT still prefers his eye-tracker for everyday use over our current BCI approaches, exploring communication via BCI remains important for two reasons.
On the one hand, as WT reported, the control of the eye-tracker becomes more and more imprecise and tiresome, hence an alternative vision independent system for communication is highly desirable.
On the other hand, early and frequent BCI practice with non-visual modalities may facilitate its continued use once the patient might lose reliable control of eye movements.
In the offline comparison, FGMDM and tangent-space logistic-regression approaches combined with xDawn achieved higher mean accuracies than the SWLDA reference.
Thus, we will consider these algorithms for future work.
We recommend evaluating xDawn together with the chosen classifier, because it improved mean accuracy for most approaches with a few exceptions.
For future evaluation, the strongest candidates were FGMDM_xDawn and TS_LG_xDawn, and TS_LG_res_xDawn.
The calibration schedule may also be evaluated, as with three calibration sessions (Trans3) competitive mean accuracy was achieved.
Because training data quantity and the number of source sessions increased together, their individual contributions to this improvement could not be determined.
ShrinkLDA remains a candidate where computational resources are limited.
Nonetheless, no classifier exceeded 70% accuracy in every evaluated session.
Our findings highlight the importance of classifier selection and the need for further improvement in the overall classification process.
Future research should emphasize BCI data collection in daily life at the enduser's home, preferably those in the LIS.
